Chapter 2: The Power and Responsibility of Individuals
You know, while institutions and laws definitely matter, it’s often the everyday choices of regular people that really decide whether democracy stays strong or starts to crumble. If you look back through history, you’ll find all sorts of stories where a single person, just by standing up—or even by quietly refusing to join in—helped tip the balance. So, what does that tell us? It means each of us has a part to play in pushing back against tyranny. One of the biggest ways we can make a difference is by refusing to help normalize oppressive behavior. Think about it: when folks see their neighbors or coworkers going along with new, unfair rules or hateful talk, it suddenly seems a lot easier for everyone else to just accept it too. That’s why, even something as simple as not joining in—or quietly questioning what’s happening—can have a real impact. Imagine one person refusing to salute a dictator, or not wearing a symbol of hate. That small act can spark others to stop and think, “Wait, should I go along with this?”
Professional ethics matter just as much. When things get tough, people in authority—like judges, doctors, teachers, even police—might feel pressure to break their own ethical codes. But when they stand firm, they become a kind of shield against abuse of power. On the other hand, if they give in, they risk becoming part of the problem.
Crises—real or invented—are often used by those who want more power to justify extreme actions. During these moments, it’s crucial to stay calm and a little skeptical. Sure, leaders might say, “We need these special powers for everyone’s safety.” But history shows that once emergency powers are handed over, they’re not so easy to take back.
And for those whose jobs involve force—like the military or police—the stakes are even higher. It’s important for them to remember that their loyalty should be to the people, not any one leader or political party. Taking a moment to think about the real consequences of their actions—and being willing to refuse unlawful or immoral orders—can truly change the course of events.
So, what can you actually do? Here are a few practical steps:
Stand out. Don’t be afraid to resist, even if it’s just in small ways, when everyone else seems to be going along.
Remember professional ethics. Stick to your principles, especially when the pressure’s on.
Be calm in a crisis. Don’t just accept drastic measures without asking questions.
And if you carry real power— like in the military or police—always reflect on the moral weight of your decisions.
Every individual choice adds up. Even the smallest acts of resistance can spark a ripple effect, inspiring others and helping to protect the values that keep a democracy alive.
